results.prompt: Our new CFO asked a yes or no question before the audit kickoff: does Fennick have any customers in sanctioned countries? I told him no because we block those at signup, and now I'd like to be sure before that goes in writing. The signup form takes a billing address and a card, self-serve accounts give us nothing else, the free tier just needs an email, nine resellers report revenue to us monthly but not end customer names, and a handful of enterprise accounts are holding companies registered somewhere other than where they operate. Give me an answer I can stand behind.
results.why: Proving the absence means chasing unrelated evidence trails (self-serve signals, reseller end customers, free tier, corporate structures) that no single system covers.

baseline.response:
# Can Fennick say "no customers in sanctioned countries"?

**Short answer: not yet.** The signup block is a real control, but it only covers one channel, and even there it only checks what the customer types in. Right now you can defend a narrower statement. Below is the plan to turn it into a full answer, and wording you can send the CFO today.

## Assumptions
- Fennick is US-based, so the main rules are OFAC's. EU and UK rules also apply if you have entities or significant sales there.
- "Sanctioned countries" means places under full embargo: Cuba, Iran, North Korea and the occupied Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk regions. Russia, Belarus and Venezuela are only partly sanctioned. The list changes (Syria was mostly lifted in 2025), so outside counsel confirms the current list before any other step.
- The audit will also ask about sanctioned *people and companies* (the SDN list and the 50% ownership rule), not just countries. We'll answer both at once.
- Free users count. Giving a free service to someone in an embargoed country can still be a violation.

## Why "we block at signup" doesn't settle it
1. **The control itself is unverified.** We need to know which country list it uses and when it was last updated. It may block countries but miss regions like Crimea, which have to be caught by postal code. It may run in the browser only rather than on the server. And it may not re-check when a customer changes their address later.
2. **It trusts the address the customer types in.** It doesn't compare that against the card's issuing country or the customer's IP address.
3. **It doesn't cover existing customers.** Accounts created before a country was added to the list were never checked.
4. **It doesn't touch three of your four channels:** free tier, resellers and enterprise.

## The plan, by channel (run in parallel)

| Channel | What we check | Evidence produced |
|---|---|---|
| **Self-serve paid** | Review the signup check's code and settings, and test it with addresses in each sanctioned place. Re-check every current account against today's list using billing address, card issuing country, recent login IPs and any tax ID. Flag accounts where those disagree. | Test results, plus a count of flagged accounts and how each was resolved |
| **Free tier** | Pull the last 12 months of signup and login IPs and look them up against the list. Also flag email domains like .ir, .cu, .kp, and flag heavy use of VPN or datacenter IPs. | Counts by country and a list of accounts to review |
| **Resellers (9)** | Read each contract for sanctions and export clauses that pass down to end customers. Check that each reseller isn't itself on the SDN list or in a risky country. Ask each for a signed sanctions statement and a revenue breakdown by end-customer country. If product usage can be tied to a reseller's accounts, geolocate it. | Contract gap list, statements received, usage-by-country data |
| **Enterprise holding companies** | For each account: list the true owners (anyone over 25%, adding up holdings under the 50% rule), where it actually operates, invoice and delivery addresses, and where its users log in from. Screen owners and entities against the SDN list and the EU and UK lists. | A file per account with pass, fail or open |
| **All billing entities** | Screen every paying company name against the sanctions lists with a commercial screening tool, and record the date. | Screening report |

**How I'd run it:** one agent per channel above, all working at the same time. Two to verify the signup control (code review, then testing against the real signup flow), one each for the free tier, resellers and enterprise, and one for screening all billing entities. I'd then combine the results into a single findings memo with a count, sample records and the open items for each channel.

**Before anything is written up:** run this under counsel's direction, so it's covered by legal privilege. If a real hit turns up, the options include a voluntary self-disclosure to OFAC, and counsel should decide that before the finding is in an email thread. Any confirmed hit gets access suspended right away and the payments on hold.

**Rough timing:** 1–2 weeks. Self-serve and free tier are just data queries. Most of the wait is on reseller replies and ownership records for the enterprise accounts.

## What to send the CFO now
> "Correction to my earlier answer: our self-serve signup blocks billing addresses in comprehensively sanctioned jurisdictions, but that control doesn't cover free-tier users, our nine resellers' end customers, or the beneficial ownership of enterprise holding-company accounts. We're running a full review under counsel covering all channels and will have a documented answer by [date]. We have no known sanctioned-country customers today, but I don't want to certify 'none' until that review is done."

If the review comes back clean, your final statement can be a clear "no," backed by a record of how you checked each channel. That's what an auditor actually wants to see.

toli.response:
**Restate:** The CFO asked a yes/no question and it's about to go in writing for the audit. The unstated problem is that "we block at signup" only covers one of five ways a customer reaches Fennick. For resellers, our own data can't prove "no" at all.

**Gate:** Fan out. Five criteria fire:
- **Sources:** signup code, the paid accounts, the free tier, 9 resellers and the enterprise registries are all separate places to search.
- **No list:** nobody has a list of accounts that might be in a sanctioned country. It has to be built.
- **Coverage:** the CFO is signing off on "none" being complete.
- **Judgment:** one agent would be too quick to agree that "we block it" settles it.
- **Depth:** each reseller and each holding company is its own investigation.

**Assumptions:**
- These are connected: the data warehouse (signups, billing, login IP logs), the payment processor (which country issued the card), CRM, the contract repository and the code host.
- "Sanctioned country" means the full US embargo programs as of the run date: Cuba, Iran, North Korea, and the Crimea, DNR and LNR regions of Ukraine. Syria's status is checked when the run starts. Counsel can swap in their own list.
- "Customer" means any account with usage or billing during the audit fiscal year.

```
INTENT   "any customers in sanctioned countries?" -> yes / no-known / can't-confirm, per channel, with evidence and gaps named
BAR      An account counts if, during the audit year, it had use or billing tied to an embargoed
         jurisdiction by any one signal: billing address, card-issuing country, repeated logins
         from there, the reseller's own location or territory, or where a holding company
         actually operates or who ultimately owns it. Crimea/DNR/LNR are matched by region and
         postal code, not the country code. Excluded: Russia/Belarus (restricted, not
         embargoed), which get their own list outside the yes/no; one-off travel logins.
SHAPE    Diamond, fixed explorers + coverage refuters   (not Pipeline: the deliverable is one merged
         answer, not a verdict per item; it flips if the CFO wants a table per account instead)

         control ──┐
         selfserve─┤                         ┌▶ 3 refuters / candidate ─┐
         free ─────┼▶ consolidate (code) ────┤                          ├▶ answer
         9 resellr─┤  dedupe by account,     └▶ 5 coverage refuters ────┘
         E enterpr─┘  threshold, cap C≤8      (barrier)

COST     up to 50 agents (3 channel explorers + 9 reseller + E≤8 enterprise explorers
         + 3 refuters × C≤8 candidates + 5 coverage refuters + 1 synthesis) · depth 3 · max 10 concurrent
         · explorers effort low, refuters default, synthesis high, no model tiering
         Moves with E (holding companies, one CRM query) and C (candidates that pass the code threshold).
WATCH    The reseller explorers. We don't have end-customer names, so "found nothing" there means
         there was no data, not that the resellers are clean. That channel cannot come back as
         a confirmed no without written statements from the resellers.
```

At most 50 agents, over the 15-agent ceiling. Say `cheaper` for 3 trims or `go` to run as-is. This answer goes to the CFO and the audit, so the full plan follows.

**why:** Five channels, each checked a different way, feed one yes/no. That's divergent exploration merged into one answer, which is the Diamond shape. The consolidate step is plain code: it dedupes flags by account ID, ignores logins that appear only once, and caps the list for verification.

There are two refuter layers. Candidate refuters try to disprove "this account is in a sanctioned country." A refuter can only rule an account out by quoting the evidence that clears it. If it can't, the account stays unresolved. Coverage refuters attack each channel's "zero" by hunting for a way in nobody checked: API signups, accounts created by admins, addresses edited after signup, accounts that predate the block.

If the shape is wrong: with Pipeline you'd get 20 separate verdicts and nobody would own the rollup. With a single pass you'd get "no" because the block exists.

**who:**
- **Explorers:** `Explore` (read-only), effort low, extraction only. They return evidence rows, not verdicts.
  - The control explorer reads the signup code and its git history.
  - The self-serve and free-tier explorers use the warehouse and the payment processor. The free tier has only an email, so they use signup/login IPs and email country domains (.ir .cu .kp .sy).
  - Reseller explorers use the contract repository, CRM and the monthly revenue reports, plus login IPs on licenses provisioned through each reseller.
  - Enterprise explorers use CRM, invoices, login IPs and corporate registries on the web, looking for where each company actually operates and who owns it.
- **Plain code, no agent:** looking up the sanctioned list, filtering by country or region, the login-frequency threshold, deduping and the cap.
- **Refuters:** default agent type, default effort.
- **Synthesis:** effort high.
- **Isolation:** none, since everything is read-only.

**scope:**
- **In:** all accounts active during the audit fiscal year, across all five channels, plus the signup block's contents, where it's enforced and when it was added.
- **Cut:**
  - Checking names against the US sanctioned-persons list is a different question. It's reported as a follow-up.
  - Enterprise explorers are capped at 8. If there are more, the extras are listed as unprocessed.
  - Only 8 candidates get refuters. Any candidate past 8 is listed as flagged and unverified, and that alone turns the answer into can't-confirm.
- **Not done by the run:** asking resellers for written statements. That goes outward, so I'll draft the request but won't send it without your OK.

**prompts (condensed):**
- **Self-serve explorer:** "Query the audit-year accounts in the warehouse and the payment processor. Return {account_id, signal, value, quote/row} for each: billing country or region in LIST, card-issuing country in LIST, 3 or more logins from LIST, or a billing address changed to LIST after signup. Crimea/DNR/LNR are matched on region and postal code. Russia/Belarus go in `restricted`, not hits. Don't judge. An empty array is valid and common."
- **Reseller explorer (×9):** "Reseller {name}. Extract its registered and operating country, the territory and sanctions clauses in its contract (quoted), any geography in its revenue reports, and login countries on licenses provisioned through it. Return {reseller, hq, territory_quote, sanctions_clause_quote, geo_signals[], data_gap}. `data_gap` must say what we can't see. Don't conclude clean."
- **Enterprise explorer (×E):** "Account {name}. Extract country of registration, country of operation (invoices, ship-to, where logins come from) and ultimate owners from registries, each with a source. Return a flat record. Being registered offshore is not a hit by itself."
- **Candidate refuter (×3):** "Try to refute that {account} is tied to {LIST} by {evidence}. Answer `refuted` only with quoted evidence that clears it (such as a VPN pattern or a verified address somewhere else). Answer `confirmed` only if it survived a real attempt. Otherwise `unresolved`."
- **Coverage refuter (×5):** "Channel {X} reported zero. Find a way a sanctioned-country customer could have got in that the explorer didn't check. Return {bypass, evidence_quote, checked: bool}. An empty array is valid."
- **Synthesis:** returns {answer: yes | no_known | cannot_confirm, per_channel[], confirmed[], unresolved[], unverified_overflow[], restricted_not_embargoed[], gaps[], complete, processed, unprocessed, stop_reason}.

**cheaper:**
1. **Single pass, no fan-out (about 0 agents):** I run the self-serve, free-tier and signup-block checks myself. You get a solid answer about direct customers only. Resellers and holding companies are marked unchecked, and nothing gets adversarially tested.
2. **One judge per candidate instead of 3 refuters (up to 34):** cheaper, but one agent is more likely to wave through a real hit as "travel."
3. **Drop the 9 reseller explorers and rely on written reseller statements alone (up to 41):** the reseller part of the answer then rests only on what the resellers tell us, and the contract review is lost.

Two things you should know before `go`, whatever the results:
- **Resellers:** the most you can put in writing today is "no known customers in sanctioned countries through direct channels." Resellers can only move to a clean "no" once their statements come back.
- **Russia/Belarus:** if Fennick sells software services there, the separate Russia/Belarus list may matter to the auditors even though it isn't part of the yes/no.

`go` · `go but <change>` · `cheaper`

results.prompt: Q4 partner rebates pay by tier and finance can't claw money back once it's wired, so I need the right tier for each of Fennick's 84 partners by Friday. The partner portal, the public directory page, the deal registration form and the channel team's tracker disagree on maybe a dozen partners, and three channel managers have each told me their version is the real one. Tier changes are only ever made in the PRM. The portal and the registration form read it live, the directory is a static page someone rebuilds when they remember, and the tracker started as a PRM export in August that people have been editing since.
results.why: Every disputed source is a stale copy of the PRM, so one export from the system of record settles all 84 with no independent investigation.

baseline.response:
The PRM is the answer, not a vote among the four sources. Tier changes only happen in the PRM, and the portal and registration form read it live, so they're really just views of it. The directory is an old copy and the tracker is an August export that people have edited by hand. When they disagree with the PRM, that tells you how the copies drifted. It doesn't tell you the correct tier.

## Assumptions
- I can read the PRM through its API or reports, including each partner's change history (who changed the tier, when, and from what to what).
- The rebate terms say which date the tier counts from (for example, the tier in effect at quarter end). If they don't, finance or the program owner picks that date before anything is paid. I won't pick it.
- The tracker has edit history (Sheets or Excel revisions), and I can find out when the directory was last rebuilt.
- I match partners by PRM partner ID, not by name.

## Plan

**1. Pull tiers from the PRM (day 1).** Export all 84 partners with partner ID, current tier, last-modified date and full tier history, and record when the export was taken. Before relying on it, make sure I'm reading the field the portal actually shows. PRMs often have look-alike fields such as "requested tier" or "next-period tier."

**2. Check the export against the live views.** For every partner, the portal and the registration form should match the export. If one doesn't, I'm reading the wrong field, a cache is stale, or a view maps tiers incorrectly. I'd fix that before going further, because it would mean my "source of truth" pull is wrong.

**3. Explain each difference.** Compare the directory and the tracker to the PRM and give every mismatch one of these causes:
- **Directory is stale:** the PRM change happened after the last rebuild. Expected; nothing to decide.
- **Tracker was edited by hand:** use revision history to find who changed it, when and what. There are two cases:
  - Someone recorded a tier change that was agreed but never entered in the PRM. This is probably what the three channel managers mean.
  - A mistake, or a change that was later reversed in the PRM.
- **Tier depends on the date:** the PRM tier changed between the rebate's effective date and today. Use the tier from the change history as of that date, not today's value.

**4. Settle the disputed partners with evidence.** Give each of the three managers one row per disputed partner: PRM tier as of the effective date, the change history, and the tracker edit history. If someone thinks the PRM is wrong, they file the change through the normal PRM process. Whether a late change counts for Q4 is for the channel lead or finance to decide in writing. I won't decide it and neither will the managers.

**5. Deliver by Thursday.** An 84-row table: partner ID, name, tier for payout (PRM as of the effective date), time of the PRM pull, the directory and tracker values, and the reason for any mismatch. Unresolved partners go in a short separate list that needs sign-off. Right before the payment file is built, pull the PRM again and compare, so a change made this week doesn't slip through.

**6. Afterwards (not blocking Friday).** Rebuild the directory from the PRM, and remove the tier column from the tracker or replace it with a live PRM lookup, so this doesn't happen again next quarter.

## Execution
This is small (84 rows), so mostly I'd do it directly. I'd run three parallel agents only for the independent pulls: the PRM export with history, the portal and form check, and the directory and tracker revision history. Sorting mismatches into causes and writing the sign-off list stay with me in one pass, because that's where mistakes would cost real money.

**Stop before wiring if:** the portal or form still disagrees with the PRM, the rebate terms don't give an effective date, or any disputed partner lacks a documented decision.

toli.response:
**Not a fan-out.** It fails the gate on sources and depth. You have 84 partners, but there is only one authoritative source: tier changes are only ever made in the PRM. Every other surface is a copy of it: two read it live, one is stale by design, and one is an edited export. Each partner's tier is a field read, not its own investigation, and one source doesn't split unless each item needs its own judgment. That avoids about **120 agents** (84 per-partner reconcilers + 3 refuters × ~12 disputed partners). The inline alternative is one PRM export, a diff in code, and a short list of human decisions.

**Assumptions**
- The rebate tier is the partner's PRM tier as of the Q4 program's qualifying date, not necessarily today's tier. If the rebate terms name a snapshot date, that date wins.
- The PRM keeps tier change history (audit log or field history).
- The channel managers' "real versions" are what they believe the tier should be. They are not evidence of what the tier is.

**Plan (one pass, today)**
1. **Export from the PRM.** Pull all 84 partners with current tier, tier change history and who made each change. Work out each partner's tier as of the qualifying date. This is the payout list.
2. **Diff in code against the other three.** Label each disagreement by cause:
   - **Directory is stale.** Expected. Compare against the last rebuild date and ignore it.
   - **Tracker was edited after the August export.** Someone edited the tracker but never changed the PRM. This is the likely source of the three competing versions.
   - **Portal or registration form differs from the PRM.** These read the PRM live, so they shouldn't differ. If one does, it's reading a different field, a cached value or another program's tier. Look into it before trusting either one.
3. **Turn the disputes into decisions, not a vote.** For each partner where a channel manager claims a tier the PRM doesn't show, the question is whether the PRM should have been updated before the qualifying date. That's for channel ops or the program owner to decide, with the tracker edit history and the qualifying criteria in hand. If the answer is yes, the change gets made **in the PRM**, dated and logged. You don't pick between spreadsheets. Set a cutoff (say Wednesday end of day) so finance has a frozen list by Thursday.
4. **Freeze and hand off.** After the cutoff, re-export the PRM with a timestamp. Finance wires from that file only. Attach the dispute log (partner, claimed tier, PRM tier, decision, who decided) so any later challenge is answered from the record, not memory.

**Watch:** "as of when." If the tier changed in the PRM during Q4, today's tier and the qualifying-date tier differ, and wiring on the wrong one can't be undone. Settle the snapshot date before the diff, not after.

At execution time I'd also add the refusal line to `~/.toli/log.jsonl` (`gate: refuse`, `agents_avoided: 120`).

results.prompt: We want to switch on the customer referral program in Germany, Brazil, Japan, Canada and the UK next quarter, same as the US one: $500 cash to the referrer when the referred company signs. Legal signed off on the US version two years ago and said the mechanics are the same everywhere. Before I brief the regional marketing leads, tell me what has to change per market. Things that have come up: our Brazil people are hired through an employer of record, the Japan team says corporate buyers there can't personally accept anything, someone mentioned German rules about incentives to employees of a customer, and finance asked how we'd even pay an individual in five currencies.
results.why: Each market carries its own independent legal, tax and payment questions with different sources and no shared answer, so the five checks are genuinely separate research.

baseline.response:
# Customer referral program: what changes in each market

**Bottom line:** Don't tell the regional leads it's "same as the US." The sign-off from two years ago covered US law only, so it can't tell you whether this works in Germany, Brazil, Japan, Canada or the UK. The issues people raised aren't one-off quirks; most of them are the same problem showing up in different places. A cash payment to a person, triggered when a company signs, can look like a bribe if that person works at the buyer. Fix that once in the global design, then adjust each market. This is a planning view, not legal advice. Each market needs a short review by a local lawyer before launch.

## Assumptions
- Referrers are mostly people who work at existing customers or partners, not the general public.
- We have no local legal entity in Brazil. The employer of record (EOR) usually means that.
- "Next quarter" means Q4 2026, which starts in about two weeks. That's too soon for five local legal reviews, so I'm assuming a staged launch.

## Global changes (apply everywhere, including the US)

1. **Who can receive cash.** Cash only goes to referrers who don't work for the company they referred, aren't public officials or employees of state-owned companies, and aren't our own staff, including Brazil's EOR staff.
2. **Referrers who work at a company (customer or partner).** They don't get cash personally. The reward goes to their employer, preferably as a credit on its account, or as a donation to a charity. We tell the employer in writing. This one rule deals with the German issue, the Japan issue, Canada's secret-commissions rule and the UK Bribery Act.
3. **How the introduction happens.** The referrer shares a link or introduces the contact themselves. We don't take the contact's details and email them. That avoids most of the data-protection and anti-spam problems (GDPR and Germany's unfair-competition law, the UK's PECR, Canada's CASL, Brazil's LGPD, Japan's APPI).
4. **When we pay.** Pay once the contract is signed and the first invoice is paid, with a clawback period. Anyone who influences the buyer's decision is excluded. Put a cap per referrer per year. Written terms must be translated locally.
5. **How we pay.** Use a global payouts provider such as Tipalti, Tremendous or Wise, not our accounts-payable process. The provider handles identity checks, sanctions screening, tax forms (W-8BEN for non-US people) and payment in EUR, BRL, JPY, CAD and GBP. Set rounded amounts in each local currency once a year instead of converting $500 each time. Account credits for employers need no payment at all, only a credit memo. That's also why credits beat paying the employer a referral fee, which would bring in vendor setup and VAT or consumption tax on the fee.

## Per market

**Germany**
- The rule someone mentioned is §299 of the criminal code (StGB) on commercial bribery. It covers giving a benefit to a customer's employee so they favor you in a purchase. Paying cash to someone at the referred company is exactly that.
- So anyone employed by a company follows rule 2 by default.
- Any emails we send must have proper consent (§7 of the unfair-competition law, UWG, plus GDPR).
- Cash paid to individuals is taxable income for them. Tell them in the terms.
- Terms in German.

**UK**
- The Bribery Act applies, including section 7, a strict-liability offence for failing to prevent bribery. Our defence is having "adequate procedures." The exclusions, the disclosure to employers and a record of approvals are those procedures, so write them down.
- UK GDPR and PECR apply to referral emails.
- Cash to individuals is taxable income for them.

**Canada**
- Criminal Code s.426 (secret commissions) targets rewarding someone's employee without their employer knowing. Rule 2 and the disclosure letter cover it.
- If we email the referred contact, CASL's referral exemption needs the referrer's full name in the message and a relationship with both sides. The link-based flow in rule 3 avoids this.
- Quebec requires French terms and marketing (Bill 96) and has its own privacy law (Law 25).
- Ask tax whether we must issue T4A slips (Canada's report for payments to individuals).

**Japan**
- The team is right that buyers won't accept money personally. Company work rules and norms make it a non-starter, so run Japan entirely on rule 2 (credit to the employer or a donation) and don't offer cash to individuals.
- Employees of state-owned or quasi-public bodies, such as national universities, count legally as public officials under Japan's bribery law. Exclude them outright.
- Terms and program materials in Japanese.

**Brazil**
- The EOR matters in two ways:
  - **Our staff can't take part.** Any referral reward for EOR staff has to go through the EOR's payroll with employment charges, or it's hidden pay. Exclude them and use an employee referral scheme instead.
  - **We have no local entity.** Payouts come from abroad as foreign-exchange payments (the provider handles this), and recipients declare the income themselves. Get a tax check that this doesn't create a taxable presence for us in Brazil if the EOR staff actively drive the program.
- Brazil's Clean Company Act and the US FCPA make public-sector buyers and state-owned companies (Petrobras, Banco do Brasil and similar) high risk, so exclude them.
- Don't add any prize-draw element. That would need government authorization under Law 5.768.
- Terms in Portuguese.

## Rollout
- **Brief the leads now** on the global structure and tell them the timing is still to be confirmed. No public launch anywhere until local counsel has signed off in that market.
- **Suggested order:** UK and Canada in Q4 (closest to US law and fastest to review), Germany next, Japan and Brazil in Q1 2027 (Japan needs the employer-reward-only design, Brazil needs the EOR and tax questions resolved).
- **Finance:** pick the payouts provider and set the local amounts in parallel with the legal reviews.

At execution time I'd run one research agent per market in parallel. Each would produce a list of specific questions for local counsel plus draft local terms. A final pass would check them against the global rules above. Counsel still makes the actual legal call.

toli.response:
**Restating the ask:** you want a per-market list of what has to change before the US referral program ($500 cash to the referrer when the referred company signs) launches in DE, BR, JP, CA and the UK. There's also a constraint you didn't state. Legal said "the mechanics are the same everywhere," and that claim is the thing under test, not something to build on. A sign-off given for the US two years ago says nothing about UK, German or Canadian bribery law, Japanese premium rules, or how Brazil pays out.

**Gate: fan out.** Three criteria fire:
- **Depth:** each market is its own dig, with a different bribery law, tax authority, payout method and internal setup.
- **Sources:** US legal memo, local law and tax sources, the Brazil EOR contract, finance's payment provider, and the chat threads where these issues came up.
- **Judgment:** a single agent will go along with "legal said it's the same."

Five markets is exactly five, so the item count alone would not have tipped it. The final brief has to agree with itself, so the research runs in parallel and the brief is written in one pass.

**Assumptions:**
- The referrer is an individual working at an existing customer.
- A US entity pays.
- Brazil has no legal entity of ours (that's why staff are on an EOR), and possibly other markets don't either.
- The US memo is in ~~docs.
- The output is a list of issues for legal to sign off, not a legal clearance.

**What I expect, unverified:**
- Cash to a customer's employee that depends on a deal closing is the textbook commercial-bribery pattern under the UK Bribery Act (including the company's liability for failing to prevent it), German §299 StGB and Canada's Criminal Code s.426.
- Japan's premium rules and buyers' own compliance policies point the same way.
- If so, the brief is one redesign (for example, credit to the customer's account or a donation, with the employer told and agreeing), not five local tweaks.

```
INTENT   US referral mechanics + 5 target markets -> per-market list of required changes (blocker / must-change / confirm with counsel), each with quoted evidence
BAR      A "change" is any part of the US mechanics that a market's law, tax or payout rules, or our own setup there, makes unlawful, taxable in a way we'd miss, or impossible to run. The parts: who can refer, what the reward is, how much, what triggers it, who is told, which entity pays, how it's paid, tax reporting, handling of the referred contact's data. Excludes translation, local copy and nice-to-have tweaks.
SHAPE    Pipeline, with a sequential head and one synthesis barrier   (not Diamond by legal topic: flips if 3+ markets hit the same blocker, since then the answer is one cross-market redesign and one worker per topic beats one per market)

         US memo: what legal assumed (1) ─▶ 5 markets
            ├─ DE: extract ─ judge ─ 3 refuters ─┐
            ├─ BR: extract ─ judge ─ 3 refuters ─┼─▶ brief (one pass)
            └─ JP · CA · UK  (same chain)        ┘   (only barrier)

COST     27 agents (1 memo reader + 5 markets x [extract + judge + 3 refuters] + 1 synthesis) · depth 5 · max 15 concurrent · extract runs Explore at low effort; refuters use three lenses (bribery / tax & payout / does "same as US" hold); synthesis at raised effort
WATCH    Judge verdicts of "no change needed." The likeliest error is a market coming back clean because the US memo seemed to cover it. Also: no connected tool reaches local counsel, and the Brazil EOR contract may not be in any connected system. Either gap gets flagged in the output as not searched, never counted as clear.
```

27 agents, over the 15 ceiling. Say "cheaper" for 3 trims or "go" to run as-is.

**How each market gets checked:**
- **Extract:** pulls quoted evidence on commercial bribery, promotion and premium rules, how the recipient is taxed and what gets withheld or reported, payout method and FX/KYC, data protection for the referred contact, and which of our entities can legally pay.
- **Judge:** compares that evidence against the premises in the US memo.
- **Refuters:** try to kill each verdict and return refuted, confirmed or unresolved. Unresolved items go to the brief as questions for local counsel, not as clearances.

Your four known issues are seeded into the prompts:
- Brazil: EOR / no entity to pay from.
- Japan: buyers can't personally accept anything.
- Germany: incentives to a customer's employees.
- Finance: paying individuals in five currencies.

The UK and Canada get the same bribery lens even though nobody has raised it for them.

`go` · `go but <change>` · `why` · `who` · `scope` · `prompts` · `cheaper`

results.prompt: Oriel Grove pushed last week's reporting outage up to their CFO and now three people need something from me by end of day. Support wants a clean timeline of what happened on our side, finance wants the service credit figure for the invoice, and the CSM wants the apology email out tonight. Can you get all three done? The ticket thread and our status page posts have the times, their order form has the SLA table where credits are a percentage per hour of downtime past the monthly allowance, and the CSM wants the email to state both the exact outage duration and the exact credit.
results.why: The credit is derived from the timeline and the email quotes both, so the three asks are one dependent chain over a couple of short sources.

baseline.response:
The three requests depend on each other. The timeline gives the outage duration, the duration drives the credit, and the email has to quote both. If I did them separately and one source said the outage started at 14:05 while another said 14:20, the email, the invoice and the support timeline could each show a different number, and this is going to their CFO. So I'll settle one duration first and use it for everything.

## Assumptions
- The ticket thread and status page posts are the only sources of times. They may use different time zones, and the ticket may show when the customer first reported the problem rather than when it actually started.
- The order form's SLA table defines what counts as downtime, the monthly allowance, how partial hours are handled, the credit percentage, what fee it applies to, and any cap. I'll use its wording, not a general reading of "SLA credit."
- I'll produce drafts only. Finance puts the figure on the invoice, and the CSM sends the email. I won't send anything to the customer.

## Approach

**1. Pull out the facts (in parallel, 3 agents)**
- **Agent A, ticket thread:** every time-stamped event (customer report, acknowledgement, escalation, fix, confirmation), with its original time zone and a link to the message.
- **Agent B, status page:** every post (investigating, identified, monitoring, resolved), with times and exact wording.
- **Agent C, order form:** the SLA table and definitions copied word for word: what counts as downtime, the allowance (hours, or an uptime % that I'll turn into minutes for that month's length), rounding, the credit rate, the fee it's based on, the cap and any claim requirements.

**2. Timeline (me, in order)**
- Convert everything to UTC and merge it into one list. Each entry notes where it came from.
- Choose the start and end times the SLA's downtime definition calls for. Usually that's first confirmed impact to confirmed resolution, not the status page's "monitoring" post.
- Put any disagreements between sources in a short "discrepancies" note instead of quietly picking one. The result is Support's timeline.

**3. Credit worksheet**
- Show each step: duration, minus the monthly allowance, the hours that count after rounding, the rate per hour, the fee it applies to, any cap, and the final dollar amount.
- If a source disagreement or unclear SLA wording changes the result, give the figure for each reading and say which one I recommend. Finance shouldn't have to redo the math.

**4. Apology email draft**
- Short and factual: what happened, the exact duration, the exact credit and where it will show up, what we're changing, and a contact.
- The two numbers get copied straight from the worksheet. Before handing off, I'll check that they match the timeline and the worksheet exactly.
- It won't guess at root cause beyond what the timeline supports.

## What you'll get
1. A UTC timeline with sources and a discrepancies note (for Support)
2. A credit worksheet with the arithmetic and the SLA wording (for Finance)
3. A draft email with the duration and credit filled in (for the CSM)

Before the email goes out tonight, Finance should confirm the credit figure. If the sources disagree on start or end time, I'll show the difference in dollars so whoever signs off can decide quickly.

toli.response:
**Not a fan-out.** It fails the items test: there are three deliverables, not more than five, and all three depend on one set of facts. The timeline gives the duration, the duration gives the credit, and the email states both. If agents worked on each deliverable separately, they could each read the start and end times differently and send three different numbers to a CFO. Splitting it would have cost about 4 agents (one per deliverable plus one to reconcile their numbers), and it would add risk. The better approach is one pass in order, with a single set of numbers used everywhere.

## Assumptions
- The ticket thread and status page posts are both available. When they disagree on a time, the order form's definition of "downtime" decides which one counts, not whichever time came first or last.
- The reporting product is a service the order form's SLA covers. If it isn't, the credit is zero and the email changes a lot, so I check this first.
- The credit is calculated against the affected subscription's monthly fee for the month the outage happened.
- I draft the email. I don't send it: it commits us to a figure in writing, so the CSM sends it.

## Approach (in order)

1. **Read the SLA before any logs.** From the order form, get:
   - how downtime is defined (full outage only, or degraded counts too)
   - when it starts (first customer impact, detection, or first status post)
   - the monthly allowance
   - how partial hours count (prorated or rounded up)
   - any credit cap
   - which fee the percentage applies to

   These rules decide which timestamps matter, so they come first.

2. **Build the timeline.** Put every timestamp from the ticket thread and the status page in one table, all in UTC:
   - detected
   - first status post
   - mitigation
   - "resolved" post
   - actual recovery confirmation

   Wherever the two sources disagree, keep both times, pick one using the step 1 definition, and write a one-line reason. This table is Support's deliverable, lightly cleaned up.

3. **Work out the downtime.** Take the downtime under the SLA definition and subtract whatever monthly allowance is left. Check whether any earlier incident this month already used some of it. That is easy to miss, and it changes the number.

4. **Work out the credit.** Hours past the allowance, using the order form's partial-hour rule, times the percentage per hour, capped if there's a cap, applied to the right fee. Show the full calculation (inputs, rule applied, result) so finance can check it in under a minute. This is finance's deliverable.

5. **Draft the email.** Copy the duration and credit from steps 3 and 4 exactly, with no retyping and no rounding. Add a short timeline summary, the cause at the level Support is comfortable sharing, the remediation, and the apology. This is the CSM's deliverable.

6. **Check consistency.** Confirm that the duration and credit match exactly in all three documents, and that the email's duration is the SLA downtime, not the raw wall-clock time. If the email should show both, label each one.

## What to watch
- **Duration.** "Exact outage duration" in the email has to be the same number the credit was calculated from. If the email shows raw elapsed time and the invoice uses SLA downtime, the CFO will see two figures that don't match.
- **Send order.** Get finance to sign off on the credit before the CSM sends the email, so the invoice never disagrees with what we told the customer.

results.prompt: We need a new webinar platform before the Q1 campaign starts and I've got six vendors on the list. Marketing wants a proper comparison, features, pricing at our volume, CRM integration, and a couple of reference calls each, and all six reps are chasing me. One wrinkle: finance won't cut a PO this quarter for anything that isn't already on the approved vendor list, that list is a page on the wiki, and security's new vendor review queue is closed until January so nothing gets added before the campaign. Come back with a recommendation.
results.why: A single gating lookup collapses the six-way evaluation to whatever is already approved, so there is no six-way investigation to run.

baseline.response:
# Plan: webinar platform recommendation

## The constraint comes first
Finance will only buy from vendors on the approved list, and security can't add anyone before the campaign. So any vendor not on the wiki list is out for Q1, however good it is. Comparing features and making reference calls for those vendors would be wasted effort. Step one is to narrow the list, not to compare.

## Assumptions
- The approved vendor list on the wiki is current and is the list finance actually uses.
- "Q1 campaign" means Q1 2027. Today is Sept 15, so the quarter ends in about two weeks. That's tight if the PO has to go out this quarter.
- Our volume and CRM (which CRM, how many attendees and events a year) are recorded somewhere I can find, such as past event data or marketing docs. If not, I'll mark them as assumptions in the comparison.
- I can't make reference calls myself. I can prepare them and score the answers.

## Approach
1. **Read the approved vendor list (I do this myself, it's one page).** Check each of the six vendors against it, watching for parent companies and product lines (for example, a company may be approved for meetings but not webinars). Also look for vendors that are already approved and have a webinar product or add-on, even if they aren't on our six. Upgrading an existing contract is often the fastest path.
2. **Decide how to proceed based on the result:**
   - **Two or more approved:** compare only those.
   - **One approved:** check it against marketing's must-haves. If it passes, recommend it. If it doesn't, list the gaps and workarounds.
   - **None approved:** there's no comparison to run. Recommend either the best approved webinar option we already have, or asking finance and security for an exception, or starting the campaign later. Include the business case for whichever path.
3. **Research the viable vendors in parallel, one agent per vendor.** Each covers: features against marketing's must-haves, pricing at our volume (list price plus what the rep is likely to quote), how deep the integration with our CRM goes (native vs. Zapier, which fields and events sync, lead routing), and whether contract and PO timing can fit this quarter. Each agent returns the same structured table.
4. **Prepare reference calls** for the viable vendors only: 5–6 standard questions and a request for 2 customers at a similar size who use the same CRM. Ask the reps to set these up, since they're chasing us anyway.
5. **Draft replies to the reps.** Short "not moving forward this cycle" notes for vendors that aren't approved, and next-step emails for the viable ones. I won't send any of them without your go-ahead.

## What you'll get back
- A one-page recommendation: which vendor and why, with a comparison table covering only purchasable vendors.
- A "Not purchasable for Q1" section so marketing can see why their favorites were dropped.
- The PO deadline and the risks.
- If nothing on the list works, a clear call on whether to ask for an exception or change the campaign timeline, with the specific person to ask.

toli.response:
**Restate:** you need a webinar platform live for the Q1 campaign, and marketing wants six vendors compared. The hidden constraint is that anything not already on the approved vendor list can't be bought in time. Finance won't issue a PO for it, and security can't approve it before January.

**Not a fan-out.** It fails on **items**. That wiki page decides eligibility before anything else. A vendor who isn't on it can't win, however well they score. The real set is however many of the six are on the page, and that's probably 0–2. What's left is a single recommendation where the options get weighed against each other, not six separate verdicts. Running all six in parallel would cost **19 agents** (6 vendors × 3 stages: features and CRM integration, pricing at our volume, verification of the vendor's claims; plus 1 to synthesize). It would also schedule 12 reference calls, most of them for vendors finance can't pay. Instead, I'll check the list first and then compare only the eligible vendors in one pass.

**Assumptions**
- The approved vendor list is a single wiki page I can read through the docs connector. A vendor counts as approved if they're listed and not marked expired or pending.
- The quarter is the calendar quarter. It ends Sept 30, and security reopens in January, so nothing new gets approved before Q1 however it's counted.
- Reference calls are made by people, not agents. Only eligible vendors get them.

**Step 1: check the list**
Read the page and match all six names against it, including parent companies. Vendors are often listed under the company that owns them, e.g. a webinar tool under its parent's name. The result is a table of all six: approved or not, with the matching line from the page quoted.

**Step 2: what happens next depends on the count**

| Eligible | What I do | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Check whether an existing approved tool can run webinars at our volume, such as a video platform or marketing-automation suite we already pay for. Price that tier. | "None of the six can be bought before Q1. Run Q1 on [existing tool / add-on]. Put the six through the security review in January for Q2." Tell all six reps to wait. |
| **1** | Check it properly: pricing at our attendee and event volume, how its CRM integration works (native or through middleware, which fields sync, how leads get attributed), and any feature gaps against marketing's list. Set up 2 reference calls. | "Buy [vendor]. It's the only one we can buy, and here are the gaps we'd have to work around." Tell the other five to come back in January. |
| **2–3** | Compare them side by side on the four things marketing asked for: features, pricing at our volume, CRM integration, references. Use one shared scale so the scores can be compared. 2 reference calls for each. | A ranked pick with the deciding tradeoff named. The rest are told January. |

**What you get back:** a one-page recommendation with the eligibility table at the top, so marketing can see why most of the six were never scored. It also includes a short reply you can send the reps who don't qualify, which clears most of your inbox straight away.

**Watch:** the name matching in step 1. If a vendor is approved under a parent or reseller name and I miss it, a real option gets dropped. Any vendor I can't match with confidence gets flagged for you to confirm with finance before I rule it out.

Last step: I'd add a line to `~/.toli/log.jsonl` recording this as a refusal: `criteria_fired: ["depth","sources"]`, `agents_avoided: 19`.

results.prompt: A prospect told me on a call yesterday that they already buy Fennick, through a company none of us have heard of, at a price nobody here would have approved. Our reseller agreements allow appointing subcontractors with notice, and I can't find any notices. Two of our resellers also list us on cloud marketplaces, one runs a managed service where we're bundled into their per-seat price, and the Oriel Grove partnership has its own referral arrangement that predates the current agreement. Work out how our software is actually reaching customers and who is selling it.
results.why: The set of resellers and sub-resellers is not knowable up front; each one found points at further channels, so discovery has to branch across separate parties and records.

baseline.response:
# Plan: finding out who is actually selling Fennick

## Assumptions
- At execution time I can get into the contract repository, the legal notices inbox, CRM, billing and finance, our license/entitlement system and product telemetry, and our seller portals on the cloud marketplaces (AWS, Azure, GCP).
- The prospect's rep can get a small amount of detail from them: the vendor's name, a quote or invoice, and ideally a license key, tenant ID or marketplace offer ID. Contacting the prospect or any partner is outward-facing, so I'll get your sign-off first.
- The goal is to map the channels and find the problems. Enforcement (audit notices, breach letters) is a separate decision.

## Approach
Build three independent pictures and compare them. Every gap between them is an unexplained route to customers.
1. **Deployments:** what is actually running at customers (entitlements, activations, tenants).
2. **Payments:** where the money comes from (invoices, marketplace payouts, reseller sales reports, referral fees).
3. **Contracts:** what each partner is allowed to do.

I'll start from our own data rather than waiting on the prospect. The prospect's details are then a test case: the map should be able to explain their purchase.

## Parallel workstreams (one agent each, run at the same time)
1. **Contract terms.** For each reseller agreement, the managed-service agreement and both Oriel Grove documents (the referral arrangement and the current agreement), pull out:
   - rights to appoint subcontractors or sublicense
   - how notice must be given, and to which address
   - rights to list on marketplaces
   - pricing floors or approval rules
   - reporting and audit rights
   - whether the older Oriel Grove arrangement was replaced or still stands alongside the current one

   Then search every place a notice could have landed: the legal inbox, old notice addresses, former employees' mailboxes, CRM attachments and partner portal uploads. A notice that went to the wrong place is a different finding from no notice at all.
2. **Marketplaces.** Export all listings, private offers and multi-party offers (AWS CPPO, Azure multiparty private offers, GCP reseller offers), including buyer accounts, prices and authorized partners. Also search each marketplace for Fennick listings we don't own. My leading hypothesis is that the unknown company is a downstream partner authorized on one reseller's marketplace offer. That would never look like "appointing a subcontractor" to the reseller, so no notice would ever have been sent.
3. **Deployments.** List every active entitlement and tenant, joined to the order that created it. Flag:
   - activations with no matching order
   - orders whose channel doesn't match the customer's billing entity
   - managed-service customers' seat counts compared with what the managed-service partner reports to us
   - customer domains that don't match the organization that paid

   Downstream managed-service providers reselling bundled seats would show up here.
4. **Money.** Compare revenue by channel against each reseller's sales reports and marketplace payout reports. Also list Oriel Grove referral payouts: which accounts they covered, whether those accounts fall inside the original referral scope, and whether Oriel Grove appears to be using its own sub-referrers.
5. **Outside search.** Look for websites, price lists, procurement notices and partner directories offering Fennick. Once we have the unknown company's name, search it for links to any of our partners (shared directors, "partner of" pages, the marketplace offers found in workstream 2).

## Synthesis
- **Channel map:** every route from Fennick to a customer as a chain (Fennick → party → party → customer). Each link records its contractual basis, price, whether notice was given, and the evidence behind it.
- **Classification of each chain:**
  - authorized and properly noticed
  - allowed by contract, but no notice received
  - outside the partner's rights (marketplace pass-through, managed-service sublicensing, referrals beyond scope)
  - pricing breach
  - no explanation (possible grey market or misused license keys)
- **Test case:** trace the prospect's purchase through the map. If no chain explains it, that is itself the most important finding.
- **Deliverable:**
  - the channel map
  - a ranked list of problems with evidence, and how much revenue and how many customers each affects
  - contract gaps to fix (notice rules for marketplace partners, managed-service sublicensing, whether the Oriel Grove referral arrangement is still in force)
  - recommended next steps, which I will not take without your approval

toli.response:
**Restate:** You want to trace every path that puts Fennick in a customer's hands, and who sets the price on each. The unstated part is that the likely answer is a sub-reseller appointed without notice, so no contract list will show it. It has to be found from the customer and money side.

**Assumptions:** When this runs, these sources are connected: the contract repository, CRM, billing/ERP, license activation data in the data warehouse, seller portals for all three cloud marketplaces, email for subcontractor notices, and web search. There are about 8 to 12 authorized resellers. The prospect's license or tenant can be identified from the call.

**Gate:** Fan out. Four criteria fire:
- **No list:** the unknown company isn't recorded anywhere.
- **Sources:** contracts, notices, billing, license data, marketplaces and the web are separate places.
- **Depth:** each path is its own dig.
- **Coverage:** enforcement or termination decisions will rest on the map being complete.

**First step, before any agents:** I trace the prospect's license back to the order that sold it, myself. That one lookup should give us the unknown company's name to start the search.

```
INTENT   "how is Fennick actually reaching customers" -> a map of every sales path, each marked authorized / appointed without notice / no basis, with evidence
BAR      A path counts if anyone other than Fennick sets or collects the price between us and the end customer: sub-resellers, marketplace private offers, seats bundled into a managed service, paid referrals (Oriel Grove included). Each path needs a named party and a paper or money trail. Excludes implementation or SI partners who never touch the license or the money.
SHAPE    Diamond + until-dry   (not Pipeline per known reseller: it only finds what our resellers disclose, and the unknown company isn't one of them. Flips if license activations already map every customer to a specific order path)

         seed ─┬─▶ explore: contracts+notices ─┐
               ├─▶ explore: billing/orders ────┤
               ├─▶ explore: activations vs contracts ┼─▶ consolidate ─▶ refute each ─▶ synthesize
               ├─▶ explore: marketplace offers ┤   (code, barrier)   unbacked path
               └─▶ explore: web listings ──────┘   rounds until dry

COST     up to 40 agents (5 explorers/round x cap 3 rounds + 3 refuters x cap 8 unbacked paths + 1 synthesis). Moves with how many paths have no authorization on file · depth 4 · max 8 concurrent · explorers Explore type at low effort, refuters and synthesis at default effort
WATCH    consolidate. The unknown company will likely show up under different names in billing, activations and marketplace offers (trading name vs legal entity). A bad identity key either splits one sub-reseller into three or hides it inside a known reseller.
```

**How the stages work:**
- **Rounds:** each round after the first targets only the new companies or customers the previous round turned up. The search stops after one round that finds nothing new, or at 3 rounds.
- **Consolidate:** plain code. It builds the chain of who sells to whom, merges duplicate names on a normalized identity key, and marks each path authorized, appointed without notice, or no basis.
- **Refuters:** each path with no authorization on file gets three, each looking from a different angle:
  1. Is there a notice or authorization somewhere we missed?
  2. Does money actually flow this way?
  3. Is the price outside approved bands?

  A refuter can only reject a path by quoting counter-evidence. Paths nobody can confirm or reject are reported separately, not dropped.
- **Already-known paths:** the two marketplace listings, the managed-service bundle and the Oriel Grove referral are handled by the explorers by source. The synthesis step then weighs the Oriel Grove terms that predate the current agreement against that agreement.
- **Limits:** agents only read, nothing is written. If either cap is hit, the output says the sweep is incomplete and lists what wasn't processed.

The run could spawn up to 40 agents, over the 15 ceiling. Say "cheaper" for 3 trims, or "go" to run it as-is.

results.prompt: 130 accounts renew in January and every one of them has to get the invoicing terms change notice at least 60 days out, so these go this week. Legal approved the template wording and it can't be edited, the only variable bits are account name, renewal date, the effective date of the new terms and the CSM's name in the signature. All four are columns in the renewal export that billing sends every Monday. A few CSMs have asked to add a personal note to their own accounts, which legal has already said no to.
results.why: It is one approved template merged against four columns of one export, mechanical for all 130 with nothing per-account to figure out.

baseline.response:
# Plan: January renewal notices for invoicing terms changes

**Approach:** A plain, deterministic mail merge done by a script. No AI writes or rewrites any of the text, and no multi-agent workflow is needed. The template is locked and only four values change, so the job is filling in those values and proving that nothing else changed. A script can prove that; generated text can't.

## Assumptions
- Input is this Monday's (Sept 14) renewal export from billing, as a CSV. It has account name, renewal date, new-terms effective date and CSM name, plus a recipient email for each account. If the email isn't in the export, I join it from the CRM using the account ID.
- Legal's template is plain text or HTML with four placeholders, and I use it exactly as delivered.
- Sending goes through the usual outbound tool (CRM or email service), which keeps a per-message send log.
- Send date is this week, around Sept 16–18. The 60-day cutoff for a Jan 1 renewal is Nov 2, so there's plenty of margin. The script still checks every row.

## Steps
1. **Filter and reconcile.** Keep only rows with a renewal date in January 2027. If the count isn't exactly 130, stop and check with billing before going further.
2. **Validate every row.** Stop the whole run on any failure rather than skipping rows:
   - All four fields and the recipient email are filled in.
   - Dates parse correctly.
   - The renewal date is at least 60 days after the planned send date.
   - The effective date is filled in and makes sense against the renewal date.
   - No duplicate accounts.
   - Each CSM name matches the CSM list.
3. **Render with a strict template engine.** A missing variable is an error. Values are escaped. There are exactly four inputs and no free-text field, so personal notes are impossible by design. Dates use one clear format (e.g. "January 15, 2027").
4. **Check the output against legal's wording.** For each of the 130 rendered notices, swap the four inserted values back to placeholders and diff against the approved template. The result must be byte-identical. Any difference fails the run.
5. **Review before sending.** Produce a review sheet (account, recipient, the four values, send date, days of notice) plus 3–5 rendered samples. Send the samples to an internal inbox to check rendering in real email clients. Get your sign-off, and legal's if they want it, before the real send. Sending to customers can't be undone, so I won't send without that confirmation.
6. **Send and keep records.** Send all 130. Then match the send log against the account list: 130 delivered, bounces followed up. Store the log, the rendered notices and the review sheet as proof of notice for each account.

## CSM personal notes
Nothing is built for them. Legal said no, and the template has nowhere to put one. I'd tell the CSMs who asked that the notice goes out exactly as approved.

toli.response:
**Restate:** You need 130 January-renewal accounts to get legal's locked invoicing-terms notice this week. The template can't change, and it has four fields, all filled from Monday's billing export. The part you didn't say out loud: you have to be able to prove that every account got the exact approved text at least 60 days ahead.

**Not a fan-out.** The depth test fails: filling four fields in from one export row is a lookup, not a multi-step investigation. The list is also already known (one file, one row per account), there's one source, and there's no judgment call. Coverage matters here, but code gives you a stronger coverage claim than agents would. The obvious pipeline would have been **260 agents avoided** (130 accounts × 2 stages: fill, then verify). It would also have added risk, because an agent can reword a locked legal template.

## Approach: a scripted mail merge with hard checks, done in one pass

**Assumptions**
- The input is this Monday's (Sept 14) renewal export.
- "60 days out" is counted from the renewal date. I'll also check it against the effective date, in case legal meant that one.
- The template exists as the approved final text with four placeholders.
- Notices go out through your existing email or CS platform, which records whether each one was delivered.

**Steps**
1. **Check the export is complete (one lookup).** Pull the count of January renewals from the CRM and compare it to the export's rows, in both directions. An account that's missing from the export is the only way this goes wrong without anyone noticing, so find it before sending.
2. **Check every row in code, and stop if any row fails:**
   - exactly 130 rows, no duplicate accounts
   - none of the four fields is blank
   - renewal dates parse and fall in January 2027
   - the effective date parses and makes sense next to the renewal date
   - the send date is at least 60 days before both dates. Today is 2026-09-15 and Jan 1 minus 60 days is Nov 2, so there's about 7 weeks of room.
   - every CSM name matches the active CSM roster
3. **Build the notices in code.** Swap the four placeholders into the approved text and nothing else. Then check each notice: with the four values taken back out, it must match the approved template exactly. There is no free-text field, so the CSM personal notes legal rejected can't get in.
4. **Proof set:** list all 130 (account, renewal date, effective date, CSM) and show 3–5 fully rendered notices. You or legal sign off once, not 130 times.
5. **Send, then reconcile.** Delivered + bounced + failed must add up to 130. Fix bounces the same week using contact details from the CRM. Keep the log of sends and delivery receipts as your record that each account was notified on time.

**Most likely to go wrong:** an account that renews in January but isn't in the export (step 1 covers this), or a CSM name that has changed since the export was made (the roster check covers this).

Log entry (it gets written to `~/.toli/log.jsonl` when this runs for real; I haven't written it in this planning session):
`{"ts":"2026-09-15","ask":"130 Jan renewal terms-change notices from locked template","gate":"refuse","criteria_fired":["items","coverage"],"agents_avoided":260}`

results.prompt: New usage limits take effect with the price change on the 1st and I want every place a customer could read them saying the same thing before that. The surfaces are the pricing page, the standard order form, the limits table in the docs, the in-app upgrade modal, and whatever the billing system actually enforces. Different teams own each of those and none of them is generated from another; the pricing page used to be built from the billing config, but the redesign last year hardcoded the numbers into the CMS. Sales has already started quoting the new limits.
results.why: Five independently authored and independently maintained surfaces with no master source each need their own read and judgment, and any pair can disagree.

baseline.response:
# Plan: make all five surfaces show the same usage limits by Oct 1

## Assumptions
- "The 1st" is Oct 1, about two weeks away. That's enough time to find differences and coordinate fixes. It's not enough time to rebuild the pricing page so it's generated from billing config again, so that's out of scope.
- Each surface lives somewhere I can read: the billing config or code, the CMS (API or rendered page), the order form template, the docs repo, and the app frontend repo. I can read and draft changes for all of them. Each owning team approves and ships its own change.
- Nobody has written down one signed-off set of new limits. Sales is quoting from something, maybe a deck or a Slack thread, and that source is the fifth version of the numbers.

## Core decision: set the reference first, then compare everything to it
The biggest risk isn't that surfaces disagree with each other. It's that sales has been quoting numbers billing won't enforce, and customers are signing on those numbers. So step one is a single reference table approved by whoever owns pricing (product or finance). It's not whatever billing currently says, and not whatever sales is saying.

The reference is one row per tier × limit, with these columns:
- limit name and tier
- value and unit (GB vs GiB, seats vs users)
- period (calendar month vs rolling 30 days)
- scope (per org, workspace or seat)
- what happens at the limit: hard block, soft warning, overage charge, or "unlimited"/fair use
- effective date and timezone
- whether existing customers keep their current limits

Most real mismatches hide in the unit, period, scope and at-limit columns, not in the headline number.

## Execution

**1. Extract the current values (parallel, read-only).**
I'd launch one agent per surface at the same time, plus a sixth for sales. Each fills in the reference table's columns from its own source and cites exactly where each value came from:
- **Billing:** config and enforcement code, including default values in code, feature flags, and plan overrides for specific customers. Where the new limits are already staged, it also records the change set and how it's set to take effect.
- **Pricing page:** the CMS content *and* the rendered live page, which can differ because of caching, other locales or currencies, and fine print in tooltips or FAQs.
- **Order form:** the current template, plus any version with a future effective date.
- **Docs limits table:** the source file, plus any other docs pages that mention limits.
- **Upgrade modal:** check whether the numbers are hardcoded, come from translation files, or are fetched from an API. If fetched, it depends on billing, and the plan should say so.
- **Sales:** the quote template or deck, plus a sample of quotes and order forms sent since sales started quoting the new limits, pulled from the CRM.

**2. Build the mismatch table.**
I'd merge everything into one table: each row is a tier × limit, each column is a surface, and every cell that differs from the reference is flagged. Mismatches go into three groups:
- **Wrong number:** a straightforward fix.
- **Meaning differs:** same number, but a different unit, period, scope or at-limit behavior. These need a decision from the pricing owner, not just an edit.
- **Contract risk:** sales quoted something billing won't enforce. This goes to the pricing owner and legal now, before anything else, because those quotes may need to be honored or corrected.

**3. Fix, with the owners.**
- For each surface I'd draft the exact change: a PR for the docs, app and billing repos, and precise before/after text for the CMS and order form.
- Each goes to its owner as a ticket that links to the mismatch table.
- Billing should be released first and switched on by the effective date. It's what customers actually hit, and the modal may depend on it.
- The other surfaces get scheduled to go live Oct 1: a scheduled CMS publish, a new order form version dated for Oct 1, a docs change merged but not released, and the modal change behind a date check or flag.
- Nothing customer-facing goes live early unless the pricing owner explicitly wants the numbers announced ahead of time.

**4. Verify against production, not source.**
- **Before the 1st:** re-run the extraction against staging and preview builds. In a staging test account, actually reach each limit to confirm what happens (block, warning or charge) and at what value.
- **On Oct 1:** re-run it against the live rendered pricing page (with the CDN cache cleared), the live docs, the modal in a real account on each tier, and billing's enforcement. The job is done when the mismatch table has no flagged cells, not when the tickets are closed.

**5. Keep them from drifting again (small, after launch).**
Commit the reference table as a file. Add a scheduled check that pulls the numbers from all five surfaces and alerts on any difference. That's a cheap substitute for the generator the redesign removed, and it's what should be proposed if anyone later wants to restore it.

## What I'd bring back to you
- The mismatch table.
- The list of sales quotes that don't match what billing enforces, with customer names and quote values.
- The decisions that only the pricing owner can make.

toli.response:
**Restate:** You want to confirm, before the 1st, that the five customer-facing limit surfaces agree with the approved new limits. The unstated constraint is that sales is already quoting, so the approved numbers are already a promise to customers. Where a surface differs, the fix goes to the surface's owner, not to the numbers.

**Gate:** Fan out. Three criteria fire:
- **Depth:** each surface is its own dig in a different system.
- **Sources:** five separate places: CMS, the order form, docs, app code and billing.
- **Coverage:** "every place says the same thing" is the launch sign-off.

"More than 5 items" does not fire, since there are exactly five, and I'm not splitting them further to get there. The result is one deliverable whose parts must agree, so the gathering runs in parallel and the comparison happens once.

**Assumptions:**
- One approved source for the new limits exists, such as the pricing decision doc or the change announcement. Before the run I read it myself in one lookup and give it to every agent as the reference. If two approved versions disagree, that is the finding, and I stop there.
- "What customers read on the 1st" means the version scheduled for the 1st: a CMS draft, a docs branch, a feature flag, or billing config with an effective date. The live version may still show old numbers, and that is expected.
- I add recent sales quotes in the CRM as a sixth read. They're not a surface you named, but if they differ from the approved doc, that's the most expensive mismatch to find.

```
INTENT   5 surfaces + sales quotes -> a table of limits per tier and metric, with every mismatch and the team that owns the fix
BAR      A surface disagrees if, for any tier and metric, the version customers see on the 1st shows a different
         value, unit, period (month vs day) or hard/soft enforcement than the approved doc. Excludes wording,
         layout, rounding the doc itself uses ("10k" = 10,000), and today's live values if a scheduled change exists.
SHAPE    Pipeline, one lane per surface, compare barrier in code   (not Parallel: it would be right only if
         reading one surface needed the others; each read stands alone)

         reference (inline) ─▶ 6 surfaces
            ├─ extract ─┐
            ├─ extract ─┼─▶ diff vs reference (code, barrier) ─▶ refute per mismatched surface ─▶ report
            └─ ...     ─┘

COST     up to 13 agents (6 extractors + ≤6 refuters, 1 per surface with any mismatch, + 1 report writer)
         · depth 3 · max 6 concurrent · billing extractor at default effort, other extractors low
WATCH    Billing extraction. "What billing actually enforces" is the enforcement code path, not the config
         file: hardcoded fallbacks, grandfathering, and whether the new numbers switch on by date or by deploy.
         A config-only read would falsely pass.
```

**How the run works:**
- **Extractors:** each reads one surface in its own tool (the CMS, the order-form template, the docs repo, the app repo plus any remote config behind the upgrade modal, billing config plus enforcement code, CRM quotes). Each returns rows of tier, metric, value, unit, period, enforcement and an exact quote. They only extract; they don't judge. "Tier not shown on this surface" is a valid answer, not a mismatch.
- **Diff:** plain code, not an agent. Rows are keyed on tier and metric and compared with the reference.
- **Refuters:** one per surface with a mismatch. Each tries to kill the mismatch, for example by checking whether the extractor read the live page instead of the scheduled one, or misread a unit. Each returns `refuted` only with a quote, `confirmed` only if the mismatch survives, or `unresolved` otherwise. Unresolved ones stay in the report as their own group.
- **Report:** confirmed mismatches grouped by owning team, then any sales quotes that differ from the approved doc.

The count moves only with how many surfaces have a mismatch. If none do, the run is 6 agents and the report is written in code.
